name: stm32flash
desc: Open source flash program for STM32 using the ST serial bootloader
why: Flashes STM32 chips over the ST serial bootloader, a useful door into talking to bare microcontrollers.

brief.what_it_is: stm32flash is an open source, cross-platform command-line flash programmer for STM32 ARM microcontrollers. It talks to the chip's built-in ST serial bootloader over a UART or I2C connection. It takes a firmware image (Intel HEX or raw binary) from a file and writes it to the chip's flash, and it can also read flash back out to a file or stdout, identify the device, erase, verify, and start execution at an address. It is written in C and runs from a terminal against a serial device path such as /dev/ttyS0 or /dev/i2c-0.
brief.why_it_exists: The README does not state a motivation in so many words. Its framing is that it is an open source flash program that uses the ST serial bootloader already built into the chips. The SourceForge scout notes call it a useful way into talking to bare microcontrollers. A reviewer on the SourceForge page said they had problems with ST's STCubeProgrammer and found stm32flash worked out of the box.
brief.how_it_works: The chip's factory-programmed ST bootloader is reached over a serial link, so no debug probe is needed. stm32flash sends the initial INIT handshake, then issues bootloader commands to identify the device, erase, write, read and verify flash. Optional GPIO or RTS/DTR sequences (-i) can drive the chip's boot pins and reset line to enter and exit bootloader mode, which is hardware dependent. The README describes it as supporting device identification, read and write to flash or RAM, auto-detection of Intel HEX versus binary input, verify with up to N retries, and software reset at exit with -R.

brief.install_notes: Beyond brew install, the README says that on most platforms you build from source by running make in the source folder, and there is also autotools support. Windows builds have a separate Build page on the wiki. Source comes from the SourceForge git repo or the GitLab mirror at https://gitlab.com/stm32flash/stm32flash. Hardware is a USB-serial adapter or a UART or I2C connection to the target chip. The Hints wiki page covers a Raspberry Pi 3 UART and pin control, Linux with CH340 USB-serial adapters, and macOS with PL2303 adapters. GPIO-based entry into bootloader mode depends on how the board is wired.
brief.standout: It drives the chip's own ROM bootloader over a plain serial line, so it needs no ST-LINK or debug probe, and it can use GPIO or RTS/DTR lines to enter bootloader mode on your own board. It is a small, scriptable single binary that lets you use a plain USB-serial adapter.
brief.status: Maintained. The wiki says stm32flash 0.7 was released 2022-03-26, and the SourceForge page lists a last update of 2025-05-25. The README says the project has been maintained by Tormod Volden since 2012. The 2025 date may reflect a file or page update rather than a new release, so the exact release cadence is not fully clear.
brief.caveats: The README makes no claim of platform limits beyond the transports, but usage depends on the chip's built-in bootloader being available and on the correct serial wiring. Entry into bootloader mode via GPIO is hardware dependent. Setup can be fiddly with some USB-serial adapters, and the Hints page exists for that reason. The SourceForge page shows only 2 reviews. One reviewer asked for a feature to scan serial ports for an STM32 in boot mode, which the README does not mention. License is GPLv2. Bug reports go to the SourceForge tracker.
quotes: Open source cross platform flash program for the STM32 ARM microcontrollers using the built-in ST serial bootloader over UART or I2C
On most platforms just run "make" in the source folder.
stm32flash was originally written by Geoffrey McRae and is since 2012 maintained by Tormod Volden.
